title: Representations over $\RR$
---

:::lede
So far we have studied actions of finite groups on complex vector spaces. In this chapter we consider actions on real vector spaces and how they sit among the complex representations. We will see that an irreducible complex representation falls into exactly one of three classes: it comes from a real representation, it carries a quaternionic structure, or its character is not real-valued. A number computed from the character, the Frobenius–Schur indicator, tells which.

Throughout, $G$ is a finite group and all representations are finite-dimensional.
:::

:::definition{16.1.1} Representation over $\RR$
A ***representation of $G$ over $\RR$*** is a finite-dimensional real vector space $V_0$ together with a group homomorphism $G \to \GL(V_0)$, where $\GL(V_0)$ is the group of invertible $\RR$-linear maps $V_0 \to V_0$.
:::

The averaging argument of Lemma [13.2.1](/notes/math-55a/13-2-maschkes-theorem-and-complete-reducibility#lemma-13-2-1) works over $\RR$. If $\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_0$ is any inner product on $V_0$, then $$\langle v, w \rangle = \frac{1}{|G|} \sum_{g \in G} \langle gv, gw \rangle_0$$ is a $G$-invariant inner product. If $W_0 \subset V_0$ is a $G$-invariant subspace, then so is its orthogonal complement $W_0^\perp$, exactly as in the proof of Maschke’s theorem (Theorem [13.2.2](/notes/math-55a/13-2-maschkes-theorem-and-complete-reducibility#theorem-13-2-2)). Hence every representation of a finite group over $\RR$ is a direct sum of irreducible ones.

Part (i) of Schur’s lemma (Lemma [13.3.1](/notes/math-55a/13-3-schurs-lemma#lemma-13-3-1)) also holds over $\RR$, with the same proof: a nonzero equivariant map between irreducible representations is an isomorphism. Part (ii) fails, because its proof needs an eigenvalue.

:::example{16.1.2} Rotations of the plane
Let $n \geq 3$, and let $\ZZ/n$ act on $\RR^2$ by letting $1$ act by the rotation $$r = \begin{pmatrix} c & -s \\ s & c \end{pmatrix}, \qquad c = \cos\tfrac{2\pi}{n}, \quad s = \sin\tfrac{2\pi}{n}.$$ Since $s \neq 0$, the rotation $r$ has no real eigenvalue, so no line is invariant and the representation is irreducible. A direct computation shows that the matrices commuting with $r$ are those of the form $\begin{psmallmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{psmallmatrix}$, so $$\End_{\ZZ/n}(\RR^2) = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} a & -b \\ b & a \end{pmatrix} : a, b \in \RR \right\} \cong \CC,$$ which is larger than $\RR \cdot \id$.
:::
